newsitem.title: USA: Clinton plunges deep into heart of Texas.
newsitem.headline: Clinton plunges deep into heart of Texas.

text.p: President Bill Clinton took his confident re-election campaign riding into Texas Friday, looking to take away from Republican Bob Dole a vote-rich state that has not gone to a Democratic presidential candidate in 20 years.

At rallies under overcast skies in Fort Worth and Longview, Clinton said his economic policies were paying dividends for the American people and boasted that he has reduced the size of government far more than his Republican predecessors.

"If you look at the results of what I said we would do and what we have done and how much better off Texas is today than it was four years ago, if the people want to give me a fair shot and look to the future, yes I think we can carry Texas, because it's right for the American people," Clinton said.

In Fort Worth's Sundance Square, named for a 19th-century outlaw called the Sundance Kid, Clinton's appearance was preceded by theme songs to old Western movies and even remarks from former House Speaker Jim Wright, a Texan who resigned under an ethical cloud in 1989. Wright attacked the Republican Congress as obstructionist and mean-spirited.

Clinton took on a folksy manner, expressing pride in the cowboy hat a supporter gave him, and telling the crowd it was OK if Dole supporters showed up: "Don't boo 'em. They're welcome here." And he had fun when the microphone briefly went dead. "Turn this thing on," he said to cheers.
He was to address a third rally later in the day in Houston and spend the evening there raising $1 million for the Democratic Party.

A Democratic presidential candidate has not carried Texas since Jimmy Carter in 1976. The state's 32 electoral votes are the third-largest prize, behind California's 54 and New York's 33, in the race for 270 electoral votes and victory.

Texas is the adopted home state of former President George Bush, the Republican whom Clinton defeated in 1992, and Bush's son is governor. Clinton lost Texas to Bush in 1992 with Texas billionaire and third-party candidate Ross Perot in third place.
A University of Texas poll Sept. 19 put Clinton and Dole in a dead heat in the state, each with 41 percent support. But Republicans dismiss it.
Clinton, his Southern accent deepening, told the rallies that Republicans talked a great deal about reducing the size of government but never did when they held the White House.

"They hated it so much, but they couldn't bear to be outside of it. It kind of tickled me. But they never did anything about it," he said in Longview. He said the federal government under him has been reduced to as small as it was when John Kennedy was president.
Doug Sosnik, White House director of political affairs, sounded a confident note, saying he did not see how Dole could get to 270 electoral votes without Texas.

"I think it would be hard for him. I'm not sure how easy it's going to be for him to hit 270. We are having a hard time figuring out what map, which states he's going after to get to 270. If he doesn't win Texas, I think it will be much harder," Sosnik told reporters.

Appearing with Clinton at the rallies was the Democratic candidate for the Senate, Victor Morales, a high school teacher who came out of nowhere to win the Democratic primary by driving a pickup truck around the state in his campaign.
He seeks to unseat incumbent Republican Sen. Phil Gramm but he is far behind in the polls and most analysts give him little chance of derailing the high-spending Gramm campaign.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Clinton considered "inappropriate" remarks Morales made recently about Republican Representative Henry Bonilla but welcomed Morales' statement of regret.
Morales had called the Hispanic-American Bonilla "a wannabe white."
"Where I grew up we called them coconuts, white on the inside, brown on the outside," Morales said.
Clinton was on the first day of a two-day campaign swing. He is to travel to Rhode Island and Massachusetts on Saturday.
